text: RCSI, Read Committed Snapshot Isolation, is different from every level covered so far in this cluster. It's a database-level setting, turned on once by whoever administers the database -- not something a session opts into.

Once it's on, every session's ordinary READ COMMITTED -- including code that never says SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL at all -- silently starts behaving differently. No application code changes, no redeploy. The query still says READ COMMITTED; the engine now fulfills that under the hood with row versioning instead of locking.

Here's what actually changes. Without RCSI, a READ COMMITTED read can be blocked by another session's uncommitted write, waiting for that writer to commit or roll back. With RCSI on, the read instead gets served a last-committed, versioned copy immediately -- no waiting at all.

The precise difference from full SNAPSHOT isolation is this: RCSI gives a fresh, newly-versioned read on every statement -- each new query in a transaction can still see a more recent committed state, exactly the way ordinary READ COMMITTED always could. SNAPSHOT instead fixes one single consistent version for the whole transaction, start to finish. RCSI still allows nonrepeatable reads and phantom reads -- it just reads without blocking.

That's why so many real production systems turn RCSI on: it needs no application code change at all, and it drops reader-writer blocking dramatically for ordinary, default-level queries. It's one of the highest-leverage, lowest-risk tuning changes available.
Next lesson, we name the pattern running underneath everything in this cluster: optimistic versus pessimistic concurrency. See you there.
